entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12240"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen22272" type="x-p"/> The first of the twelve minor prophets in the order of the canon (called "minor," not as less in point of inspired authority, but simply in point of size). The twelve are first mentioned by Jesus, the son of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus 49:10). St. Stephen, in <reference osisRef="Acts.7.42">Ac 7:42</reference> (in referring to <reference osisRef="Amos.5.27">Am 5:27</reference>), quotes them as forming one collective body of writings, "the book of the prophets." So Jerome and Melito, the first Greek father who has left us a catalogue of these books. The collection of the sacred books is by Jewish tradition attributed to the great synagogue of learned scribes formed by Ezra. Many think Nehemiah completed this collection by adding to the books already in the canon those of his own times. Malachi, the last in the series, probably aided him in determining with infallible authority what books were entitled to be ranked in the inspired canon. The chronological order differs from the canonical. Joel, about 810 B.C.; Jonah, about 810 B.C., or, as others, first, 862 B.C.; Amos, about 790 B.C.; Hosea, about 784 B.C. Hosea, the contemporary of Isaiah, Micah, and Amos, seems to have entered on his prophetical office in the last years of Jeroboam (contemporary in part with Uzziah), and to have ended it in the beginning of Hezekiah's reign, 722 B.C., that is, about sixty years in all, from 784 B.C. to 722 B.C. The prophets, however, were not uninterruptedly engaged in prophesying. Considerable intervals elapsed, though their office as divinely commissioned public teachers was never wholly laid aside. The Book of Hosea which we have constitutes only that portion of his public teachings which the Holy Spirit saw fit to preserve for the benefit of the Church. The cause of his being placed first of the twelve was, probably, the length, the vivid earnestness, and patriotism of his prophecies, as well as their closer resemblance to those of the greater prophets. His style is abrupt, sententious, and unrounded; the connecting particles are few; there are changes of person, and anomalies of gender, number, and construction. His name means Salvation. He was son of Beeri, of the tribe of Issachar, born in Beth-shemesh [Jerome]. His mention, in the inscription, of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, is no proof that he belonged to Judah: for the prophets in Israel regarded its separation from Judah, civil as well as religious, as an apostasy from God, who promised the dominion of the theocracy to the line of David. Hence Elijah in Israel took twelve stones to represent Judah, as well as Israel (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.31">1Ki 18:31</reference>). Hence Hosea dates from Judah's kings, as well as from Jeroboam of Israel, though he belonged to Israel, with whose sins and fate his book is chiefly occupied. He, however, makes incidental references to Judah. His first prophecy foretells the overthrow of Jehu's house, fulfilled on the death of Jeroboam, Jehu's great-grandson (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.12">2Ki 15:12</reference>), in Zachariah, Jeroboam's son, the fourth and last from Jehu, conspired against by Shallum. This first prediction was doubtless in Jeroboam's life, as Zachariah, his son, was only suffered to reign six months; thus the inscription is verified that "the word of the Lord came unto him in the days of Jeroboam" (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.1">Ho 1:1</reference>). Again, in <reference osisRef="Hos.10.14">Ho 10:14</reference>, Shalmaneser's expedition against Israel is alluded to as past, that is, the first inroad against King Hoshea, who began to reign in the twelfth year of Ahaz; so that as Ahaz' whole reign was sixteen years, the prophecy seems to have been given about the beginning of Hezekiah's reign. Thus the inscription is confirmed that the exercise of his prophetical functions was of such a protracted duration.<div eID="gen22272" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22271" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22273" type="x-p"/> Hosea (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>) is quoted in <reference osisRef="Matt.2.15">Mt 2:15</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Ho 6:6</reference> in <reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">Mt 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.7">12:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.9.25">Ro 9:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.26">26</reference>, quoting <reference osisRef="Hos.1.10">Ho 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.23">2:1, 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.55">1Co 15:55</reference>, quoting <reference osisRef="Hos.13.14">Ho 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.10">1Pe 2:10</reference>, quoting <reference osisRef="Hos.1.9">Ho 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>; 2:23. Messianic references are not frequent; but the predictions of the future conversion of Israel to the Lord their God, and David their king, and of the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham that his spiritual seed should be as the sand of the sea (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.10">Ho 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5">3:5</reference>), clearly refer to the New Testament dispensation.<div eID="gen22273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22274" type="x-p"/> The first and third chapters are in prose, the rest of the book is rhythmical.<div eID="gen22274" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.1.1-Hos.1.11">Ho 1:1-11</reference>. Inscription.</title> <div sID="gen22275" type="x-p"/> Spiritual whoredom of Israel set forth by symbolical acts; Gomer taken to wife at God's command: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah, and Lo-Ammi, the children. Yet a promise of Judah and Israel's restoration.<div eID="gen22275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22276" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12240"/><hi type="bold">1. The word of the Lord that came unto Hosea--</hi>See Introduction.<div eID="gen22276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jeroboam--</hi>the second; who died in the fifteenth year of Uzziah's forty-one years' reign. From his time forth all Israel's kings worshipped false gods: Zachariah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.9">2Ki 15:9</reference>), Menahem (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.18">2Ki 15:18</reference>), Pekahiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.24">2Ki 15:24</reference>), Pekah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.28">2Ki 15:28</reference>), Hoshea (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.2">2Ki 17:2</reference>). As Israel was most flourishing externally under Jeroboam II, who recovered the possessions seized on by Syria, Hosea's prophecy of its downfall at that time was the more striking as it could not have been foreseen by mere human sagacity. Jonah the prophet had promised success to Jeroboam II from God, not for the king's merit, but from God's mercy to Israel; so the coast of Israel was restored by Jeroboam II from the entering of Hamath to the sea of the plain (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.23-2Kgs.14.27">2Ki 14:23-27</reference>). <div eID="gen22277" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12241"/><div sID="gen22278" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12241"/><hi type="bold">2. beginning--</hi>not of the prophet's predictions generally, but of those spoken by Hosea.<div eID="gen22278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take ... wife of whoredoms--</hi>not externally acted, but internally and in vision, as a pictorial illustration of Israel's unfaithfulness [Hengstenberg]. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.8">Eze 16:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.15">15</reference>, &c. Besides the loathsomeness of such a marriage, if an external act, it would require years for the birth of three children, which would weaken the symbol (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.4">Eze 4:4</reference>). Henderson objects that there is no hint of the transaction being fictitious: Gomer fell into lewdness after her union with Hosea, not before; for thus only she was a fit symbol of Israel, who lapsed into spiritual whoredom after the marriage contract with God on Sinai, and made even before at the call of the patriarchs of Israel. Gomer is called "a wife of whoredoms," anticipatively.<div eID="gen22279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children of whoredoms--</hi>The kingdom collectively is viewed as a mother; the individual subjects of it are spoken of as her children. "Take" being applied to both implies that they refer to the same thing viewed under different aspects. The "children" were not the prophet's own, but born of adultery, and presented to him as his [Kitto, Biblical Cyclopædia]. Rather, "children of whoredoms" means that the children, like their mother, fell into spiritual fornication. Compare "bare him a son" (see <reference osisRef="Hos.2.4">Ho 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>). Being children of a spiritual whore, they naturally fell into her whorish ways. <div eID="gen22280" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12248"/><div sID="gen22291" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12248"/><hi type="bold">9. Lo-Ammi--</hi>once "My people," but henceforth not so (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.8">Eze 16:8</reference>). The intervals between the marriage and the successive births of the three children, imply that three successive generations are intended. Jezreel, the first child, represents the dynasty of Jeroboam I and his successors, ending with Jehu's shedding the blood of Jeroboam's line in Jezreel; it was there that Jezebel was slain, in vengeance for Naboth's blood shed in the same Jezreel (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.1">1Ki 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.21">2Ki 9:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.30">30</reference>). The scenes of Jezreel were to be enacted over again on Jehu's degenerate race. At Jezreel Assyria routed Israel [Jerome]. The child's name associates past sins, intermediate punishments, and final overthrow. Lo-ruhamah ("not pitied"), the second child, is a daughter, representing the effeminate period which followed the overthrow of the first dynasty, when Israel was at once abject and impious. Lo-Ammi ("not my people"), the third child, a son, represents the vigorous dynasty (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>) of Jeroboam II; but, as prosperity did not bring with it revived piety, they were still not God's people. <div eID="gen22291" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.title: INTRODUCTION
navigation_sections.content_plain: INTRODUCTION The first of the twelve minor prophets in the order of the canon (called "minor," not as less in point of inspired authority, but simply in point of size). The twelve are first mentioned by Jesus, the son of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus 49:10). St. Stephen, in Ac 7:42 (in referring to Am 5:27 ), quotes them as forming one collective body of writings, "the book of the prophets." So Jerome and Melito, the first Greek father who has left us a catalogue of these books. The collection of the sacred books is by Jewish tradition attributed to the great synagogue of learned scribes formed by Ezra. Many think Nehemiah completed this collection by adding to the books already in the canon those of his own times. Malachi, the last in the series, probably aided him in determining with infallible authority what books were entitled to be ranked in the inspired canon. The chronological order differs from the canonical. Joel, about 810 B.C.; Jonah, about 810 B.C., or, as others, first, 862 B.C.; Amos, about 790 B.C.; Hosea, about 784 B.C. Hosea, the contemporary of Isaiah, Micah, and Amos, seems to have entered on his prophetical office in the last years of Jeroboam (contemporary in part with Uzziah), and to have ended it in the beginning of Hezekiah's reign, 722 B.C., that is, about sixty years in all, from 784 B.C. to 722 B.C. The prophets, however, were not uninterruptedly engaged in prophesying. Considerable intervals elapsed, though their office as divinely commissioned public teachers was never wholly laid aside. The Book of Hosea which we have constitutes only that portion of his public teachings which the Holy Spirit saw fit to preserve for the benefit of the Church. The cause of his being placed first of the twelve was, probably, the length, the vivid earnestness, and patriotism of his prophecies, as well as their closer resemblance to those of the greater prophets. His style is abrupt, sententious, and unrounded; the connecting particles are few; there are changes of person, and anomalies of gender, number, and construction. His name means Salvation. He was son of Beeri, of the tribe of Issachar, born in Beth-shemesh [Jerome]. His mention, in the inscription, of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, is no proof that he belonged to Judah: for the prophets in Israel regarded its separation from Judah, civil as well as religious, as an apostasy from God, who promised the dominion of the theocracy to the line of David. Hence Elijah in Israel took twelve stones to represent Judah, as well as Israel ( 1Ki 18:31 ). Hence Hosea dates from Judah's kings, as well as from Jeroboam of Israel, though he belonged to Israel, with whose sins and fate his book is chiefly occupied. He, however, makes incidental references to Judah. His first prophecy foretells the overthrow of Jehu's house, fulfilled on the death of Jeroboam, Jehu's great-grandson ( 2Ki 15:12 ), in Zachariah, Jeroboam's son, the fourth and last from Jehu, conspired against by Shallum. This first prediction was doubtless in Jeroboam's life, as Zachariah, his son, was only suffered to reign six months; thus the inscription is verified that "the word of the Lord came unto him in the days of Jeroboam" ( Ho 1:1 ). Again, in Ho 10:14 , Shalmaneser's expedition against Israel is alluded to as past, that is, the first inroad against King Hoshea, who began to reign in the twelfth year of Ahaz; so that as Ahaz' whole reign was sixteen years, the prophecy seems to have been given about the beginning of Hezekiah's reign. Thus the inscription is confirmed that the exercise of his prophetical functions was of such a protracted duration. Hosea ( Ho 11:1 ) is quoted in Mt 2:15 ; also Ho 6:6 in Mt 9:13 ; 12:7 ; compare Ro 9:25 , 26 , quoting Ho 1:10 ; 2:1, 23 ; 1Co 15:55 , quoting Ho 13:14 ; 1Pe 2:10 , quoting Ho 1:9 , 10 ; 2:23. Messianic references are not frequent; but the predictions of the future conversion of Israel to the Lord their God, and David their king, and of the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham that his spiritual seed should be as the sand of the sea ( Ho 1:10 ; 3:5 ), clearly refer to the New Testament dispensation. The first and third chapters are in prose, the rest of the book is rhythmical.
